The corpus covers this in the NBFC Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025, but only partly. Paras 92–99 set out the requirements, though I could only read the full text of paras 92, 93, 94, 97 and 99. Para 98 is cut off after its opening clause, so its full list of training topics is not confirmed.

**Conduct and training (paras 98–99):**
- The NBFC must ensure recovery agents are properly trained to handle their responsibilities "with care and sensitivity." The visible part of para 98 names soliciting customers, hours of calling, privacy of customer information, and conveying correct loan terms.
- The NBFC must obtain each recovery agent's undertaking to abide by the code of conduct.
- Recovery agents must follow the extant Fair Practices Code for NBFCs and the NBFC's own code for collection of dues and repossession of security.
- Agents must refrain from any action that could damage the NBFC's integrity and reputation, and must observe strict customer confidentiality.

**Due diligence and accountability (paras 93–94, microfinance section):**
- "Recovery agents" covers the agencies engaged for recovery and their employees.
- The NBFC must have a due diligence process for engaging recovery agents, covering the individuals involved in recovery.
- The NBFC must ensure antecedents of agency employees are verified, including police verification, and must set the periodicity for re-verification.

**Transparency and grievances (paras 92, 97):**
- The NBFC must have a dedicated mechanism for redressing recovery-related grievances, and must disclose its details to the borrower at loan disbursal (para 92).
- Up-to-date details of recovery agencies must be hosted on the NBFC's website (para 97).

**NBFC responsibility for outsourced recovery:** The NBFC remains answerable for its agents' conduct. The directions impose the obligations on the NBFC itself (undertakings, training, verification, grievance mechanism, disclosure) rather than only on the agencies. Para 7 and its A.1 policy list also require Board-approved policies covering the Fair Practices Code and grievance redressal. The rules on recovery in paras 92–97 are framed for microfinance borrowers, so I have not confirmed how far they extend to other borrowers.

structured_content.content:
6. Reasonable security safeguards. — (1) A Data Fiduciary shall protect personal data in its possession or
under its control, including in respect of any processing undertaken by it or on its behalf by a Data
Processor, by taking reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breach, which shall include, at
the minimum, —
(a) appropriate data security measures, such as securing of personal data through encryption,
obfuscation, masking or the use of virtual tokens mapped to that personal data;
(b) appropriate measures to control access to the computer resources used by such Data Fiduciary or
such a Data Processor, wherever applicable;
(c) visibility on the accessing of such personal data, through appropriate logs, monitoring and review,
for enabling detection of unauthorised access, its investigation and remediation to prevent
recurrence;
(d) reasonable measures for continued processing in the event of confidentiality, integrity or
availability of such personal data being compromised as a result of destruction or loss of access to
personal data or otherwise, such as by way of data-backups;
(e) for enabling the detection of unauthorised access, its investigation, remediation to prevent
recurrence and continued processing in the event of such a compromise, retain such logs and
personal data for a period of one year, unless compliance with any law for the time being in force
requires otherwise;
(f) appropriate provision in the contract entered into between such Data Fiduciary and such a Data
Processor, wherever applicable, for taking reasonable security safeguards; and
(g) appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure effective observance of security
safeguards.
(2) In this rule, the expression “computer resource” shall have the same meaning as is assigned to it in
Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2000).
